digest.top_line: GETUG P05: brachy boost vs 80 Gy EBRT, 5-yr bPFS 88% vs 88.2% (p=0.90) in intermediate-risk PCa without ADT, with more late G2 GU toxicity (34.1% vs 17.9%).
digest.tldr: Prostate-only day. Intensification for intermediate-risk disease is narrowing: GETUG P05 brachy boost added late GU toxicity without bPFS gain, and NRG/RTOG 0815 STAD cut DM (HR 0.35) with OS not met, benefit concentrated in Int/High Decipher GC. Post-RP, PAM50 Luminal B selects hormonal benefit with salvage RT (GU006 MFS HR 0.27).

sites.intro: The day's theme is who needs intensification with RT: dose escalation via boost, STAD in intermediate risk, and biomarker-selected ADT or ARSI with salvage RT, plus a GUAM Delphi on GU toxicity management.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase 3 RCT**, 1:1 randomisation, **n=288**. Median follow-up **61.7 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Intermediate-risk** prostate adenocarcinoma, age 18-80, expected survival ≥10y, ECOG ≤2. Excluded T3a or greater, **any ADT**, nodal or distant disease, IPSS >15 or active IBD.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Both arms: EBRT **46Gy at 2Gy/fx** to prostate + 1cm SV. Boost arm then received **LDR 110Gy or HDR 14Gy** 1-4 wk later; control received an EBRT boost of **34Gy at 2Gy/fx** to prostate.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** 5-yr bPFS. **Secondary:** toxicities, OS, PCSS, IPSS, IIEF-5, QLQ-C30.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 5-yr bPFS **88% vs 88.2% (p=0.90)**; no benefit in GG2 or GG3. 5-yr OS 96.0 vs 92.7% (p=0.30).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute GI toxicity **lower with boost** (29.9% vs 41.2%, p=0.03). Late all-grade GU **higher with boost** (82.2% vs 63.6%, p=0.0006); late GI similar (p=0.48).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: ASCENDE-RT supported LDR boost over dose-escalated EBRT, but delivered with ADT. GETUG P05 isolates the boost question **without ADT** and finds **no bPFS gain** against an 80 Gy EBRT control.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents intermediate-risk, ADT-free pts with good urinary function treated with conventionally fractionated EBRT. Does not represent high-risk disease, boost combined with ADT, or hypofractionated or SBRT comparators.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: LDR and HDR boosts pooled, so neither modality is tested on its own. bPFS at 5 yr may be early for a dose-response difference to emerge; GG subgroup estimates not shown.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: With equal biochemical control, the decision shifts to toxicity profile and logistics: boost trades **less acute GI** for **more late GU** toxicity. Longer follow-up is needed before excluding a late-emerging bPFS separation.

studies.interpretation:
The case for brachytherapy boost in intermediate-risk prostate cancer has rested largely on the idea that biologic dose escalation beyond what conventional EBRT delivers translates into better biochemical control. ASCENDE-RT is the trial most readers carry in their heads for that argument, but it delivered boost alongside ADT in a population that skewed higher risk. GETUG P05 asks a cleaner question: with ADT removed and the comparator already dose-escalated to 80 Gy in 2 Gy fractions, does a brachytherapy boost add anything? At a median follow-up of 61.7 months, the answer on the primary endpoint is no, with 5-year bPFS of 88% vs 88.2% and no signal in either grade group 2 or grade group 3.

The absence of ADT is what makes this result informative for a radiation oncologist. Without hormonal therapy masking or delaying PSA failure, bPFS here reflects the radiation itself more directly than in trials where ADT shares the credit. That strengthens the null reading rather than weakening it. If a boost conferred a meaningful local tumor-control advantage in this population, an ADT-free design is where it should be most visible.

Several design features should temper confidence in either direction. LDR and HDR boosts are pooled, and the two differ in dose distribution and in their toxicity profiles, so a modest advantage for one could be diluted by the other. The trial enrolled 288 pts, and the source does not state the power calculation or whether the design was superiority or equivalence, which matters for how strongly a null bPFS result can be read as equivalence. Five years is also not long for intermediate-risk disease, and dose-response differences in prostate cancer have historically widened with longer follow-up. The OS difference (96.0 vs 92.7%, p=0.30) is a secondary endpoint in a population with few prostate cancer deaths expected at this horizon and should not be interpreted.

The toxicity data are where the trial does change the conversation. Boost reduced acute GI toxicity but increased late all-grade GU toxicity (82.2% vs 63.6%, p=0.0006), with late grade 2 GU events of 34.1% vs 17.9%. In a setting where biochemical control is equivalent, a durable GU cost is the dominant consideration, and it argues against offering boost by default to ADT-free intermediate-risk pts.

What the trial does not settle is how boost compares with the modern alternatives most practices now use for this population, namely moderate hypofractionation and SBRT, neither of which was tested. It also leaves open whether a specific boost modality or a higher-risk subset within intermediate risk still benefits. For now, the defensible reading is that against 80 Gy conventionally fractionated EBRT without ADT, boost adds GU toxicity without adding biochemical control at 5 years.

analysis_sections.body: Transcriptomic **PAM50 subtyping** of archived tissue from NRG/RTOG 0534 SPPORT, a three-arm salvage RT trial (Pollack, Lancet Onc 2022). Whether the biomarker analysis was prespecified is not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Post-RP, PSA 0.1-2.0 ng/mL, pT2 or pT3 N0M0, Gleason ≤9.** Analytic cohort **n=709** of 1792 enrolled; 1039 had biorepository samples, with 330 lost to RNA or QC failure.

analysis_sections.body: Arms: **PBRT alone** (n=215), **PBRT + STADT** (n=247), **PBRT + STADT + PLNRT** (n=247). Dose and fractionation not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Luminal B carried the larger ADT benefit on FFP (**p-int=.01**) and MFS (**p-int=.05**). One FFP panel shows ADT arms vs PBRT alone **HR 0.34 (0.23-0.52), p<0.001**; panel attribution not legible in OCR.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RTOG 9601 and SPPORT established ADT with salvage RT in unselected post-RP pts. This analysis asks which of those pts carry the benefit, using subtype rather than PSA or pathology alone.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-RP N0M0 pts with PSA 0.1-2.0 ng/mL receiving salvage prostate bed RT. Does not represent node-positive, PSMA-staged, or higher-PSA salvage populations.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Tissue was available for under half the trial, so the subset may differ from the randomized population. Arm-level slides do not resolve PLNRT's contribution by subtype in legible form.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Subtype appears to concentrate ADT benefit in Luminal B, raising **de-escalation** potential for non-Luminal B. It does not establish safe ADT omission, which needs a prospective selected design.

studies.interpretation:
The clinical question this analysis addresses is not whether ADT helps salvage radiotherapy after prostatectomy; RTOG 9601 and the parent SPPORT trial already argued that it does in aggregate. The question is who carries that benefit, because short-term ADT is not free for a post-RP man who often has decades ahead of him, and the trials that justified it enrolled broadly. A predictive biomarker that concentrates the benefit would let a radiation oncologist offer ADT where it moves outcomes and spare it where it does not.

On that question the result is directionally clean. PAM50 Luminal B tumors gained 31% absolute 5-year FFP from ADT against 10% in non-Luminal B, with an interaction p of .01, and the 10-year MFS difference (20% vs -3%) points the same way. Biologically this is coherent: luminal tumors are the androgen-receptor-driven phenotype, so a larger hormonal effect is what one would expect, and earlier retrospective post-RP work had linked luminal subtyping to ADT response. Randomized-trial tissue is the right setting to test it, since only a randomized comparison can separate prognostic from predictive.

Confidence should still be tempered. The cohort is the 709 of 1792 men with usable tissue, and tissue availability in a cooperative-group biorepository is rarely random; if it tracks institution, era, or tumor volume, the subset may differ from the trial that generated the parent result. The source does not state whether the PAM50 interaction was a prespecified hypothesis, and a three-arm trial offers several comparisons from which a subtype interaction could emerge. The MFS interaction sits at .05, which a skeptic would call a single borderline test rather than confirmation. A negative absolute benefit in non-Luminal B is almost certainly noise around zero, not evidence of harm.

For the RT reader the nodal question remains open. The arm-level slides suggest that in one subtype panel the three-modality arm separated from PBRT alone more clearly than STADT alone did, but the panel labels are not legible in the captured OCR, and the direct PLNRT plus STADT vs STADT comparison (HR 0.64, p=0.16) does not support a subtype-selected nodal decision. The cleaner read is about ADT, not field size.

What would make this wrong is a prospective test in which non-Luminal B men treated with prostate bed RT alone fare no better than the unselected control arm historically did, or a validation in a second salvage RT trial in which the interaction disappears. Until then this belongs alongside other genomic classifiers as a reason to weigh ADT more or less heavily in discussion, not as grounds to withhold it.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The salvage RT decision it informs is the STADT add-on: Luminal B tumors gained 31% absolute 5-y FFP from ADT vs 10% in non-Luminal B (p-int=.01). PLNRT's increment over STADT is not resolved by subtype (HR 0.64, p=0.16), so the nodal-field decision stays where SPPORT left it.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Phase III prospective **randomized** trial, **n=1493** (751 RT alone, 742 RT + STAD). Stratified by number of risk factors, ACE-27 comorbidity and RT modality. Median follow-up **9.4 y** overall, **10.3 y** in survivors.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Non-metastatic **intermediate-risk** prostate cancer with ≥1 of: Gleason 7, PSA >10 to ≤20 ng/mL, T2b-T2c; **all 3 factors with ≥50% positive cores excluded**. Median age 68, 67% single risk factor, 92% Gleason 7, median PSA 8.1 ng/mL.

analysis_sections.body: Dose-escalated **EBRT 79.2 Gy**, or EBRT + LDR or HDR brachytherapy boost; **89% received EBRT alone**. RT QA >90% per protocol or acceptable variation for contours and dose.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** overall survival. Secondary: biochemical failure, local failure, distant metastasis, prostate cancer death, salvage therapy initiation, non-prostate cancer death.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Overall grade ≥3 late AEs **similar** (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.84-1.40). STAD added grade ≥3 **cardiac** (26 vs 10), metabolic/lab (20 vs 4) and grade 3 sexual (71 vs 38) events, all p<0.01. EPIC hormone/sexual deficits largely recovered by 60 months.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The trials that established STAD with RT used doses now considered inadequate; 0815 tests whether **dose escalation makes STAD redundant**, and the DM and PCSM data say it does not. The OS null mirrors the low prostate-specific mortality of this risk group rather than contradicting the hormonal-benefit literature.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents intermediate-risk, largely single-factor Gleason 7 prostate cancer treated with dose-escalated EBRT or brachy boost. Does not represent pts with all 3 risk factors and ≥50% positive cores, or PSMA PET or genomically selected cohorts.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Local failure was a secondary endpoint but its result is not reported in source, so the in-field contribution of STAD cannot be isolated. DM and prostate-death benefits rest on **small event counts** (14 vs 40, 5 vs 19), and smaller subgroups had wide CIs.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: STAD buys **disease control and fewer prostate cancer deaths without excess non-prostate mortality** (HR 0.93), at an early QoL and late cardiac cost. Investigators could not identify a subgroup without PSA-failure or DM benefit; better selection (advanced imaging, genomics, MMAI) remains open.

studies.interpretation:
The OS null is mostly a statement about who dies of what in intermediate-risk prostate cancer. Of 446 deaths, 422 were from other causes, so even a large relative reduction in prostate cancer death (19 vs 5, HR 0.26) has little room to move an all-cause endpoint. The trial was powered on a 5-year OS gain from 90% to 93%, an HR of 0.66, an assumption that in hindsight credited this population with far more prostate-cancer-driven mortality than it carries. The observed OS HR of 0.87 points the same way as every disease endpoint, and non-prostate mortality was not increased (HR 0.93). That last point matters: the cardiac and metabolic excess seen in the AE data did not surface as excess non-cancer death at this follow-up.

For the radiation oncologist, the more consequential finding is that dose escalation did not absorb the hormonal benefit. The older trials that made STAD routine with RT were run at doses now regarded as inadequate, and a reasonable hypothesis was that 79.2 Gy or a brachytherapy boost would control enough local disease to make STAD redundant. The distant metastasis data argue otherwise: 40 vs 14 events, HR 0.35, alongside a PSA failure HR of 0.60 that held across risk-factor and comorbidity strata. That pattern suggests STAD acts at least partly on occult disease that local dose cannot reach, rather than only on in-prostate radioresistance. Local failure was a prespecified secondary endpoint, but the source does not report its result, so the in-field share of the benefit cannot be separated here.

The decision problem is absolute magnitude, not relative effect. PCSM at 14 years was 3.3% vs 2.1%, and salvage ADT 15% vs 7%. These sit on a small base in a cohort where 67% had a single risk factor and 92% were Gleason 7. Against that, STAD carried more grade ≥3 cardiac events (26 vs 10) and grade 3 sexual events (71 vs 38), with early EPIC hormone and sexual decline that largely recovered by 60 months. The investigators could not identify a subgroup without PSA-failure or DM benefit, but subgroups built on few DM events have wide intervals, and failing to detect a non-benefiting subgroup is not the same as showing uniform benefit.

What the trial does not settle is selection. Eligibility rested on clinical risk factors, staging predated PSMA PET, and no genomic classifier or MMAI score was applied. Pts with all three risk factors and ≥50% positive cores were excluded, so the unfavorable end of the intermediate-risk spectrum is under-represented, which likely biases the absolute benefit downward relative to a contemporary unfavorable cohort. The practical read is that STAD remains a shared decision in intermediate-risk disease even with dose-escalated RT: it buys fewer metastases and fewer prostate cancer deaths at a measurable toxicity cost, and OS will not arbitrate between them in this risk group. The disease-control conclusion would be wrong only if the DM and PCSM estimates, built on small event counts, shrink toward null on replication; the conclusion that OS cannot be the deciding endpoint here is secure.

With 422 of 446 deaths non-prostate, the add-vs-omit STAD decision rests on DM reduction against cardiac and sexual toxicity, not OS.

Does PSMA PET staging change STAD benefit?

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Biomarker evaluation across two **prospective post-op SBRT cohorts**, SCIMITAR (NCT03541850) and EXCALIBUR (NCT04915508). Continuous AUC and dichotomized performance at the intact **0.50** threshold, then **exploratory recalibration** targeting sensitivity >=0.65 and specificity >=0.70. AUCs bootstrapped (1,000 iterations) and pooled by fixed-effects meta-analysis.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Post-radical prostatectomy pts: SCIMITAR **100 enrolled, 89 evaluable**; EXCALIBUR **74 evaluable**. Germline DNA from saliva, scored with the unmodified intact-prostate model.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: SCIMITAR: **30-34 Gy in 5 fractions** ± pelvic nodes. EXCALIBUR: **5-fraction SBRT to the prostate bed** ± nodes. Per-cohort nodal fraction not given in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Late grade 2+ GU adverse events**, the toxicity that the source says limits broader post-op RT adoption. Grading system and follow-up not stated.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Continuous discrimination held in both cohorts, but the intact **0.50** cutoff was misaligned post-op (EXCALIBUR dichotomized AUC **<0.50**). At the recalibrated **0.25** cutoff the **pooled AUC was 0.748**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: In intact-prostate SBRT, PROSTOX Ultra predicts late GU AEs at a **prespecified 0.50** threshold. Post-op, the **risk ordering transferred** while the decision threshold moved down, which the authors attribute to context, not to a different signal.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-RP pts treated with 5-fraction prostate-bed SBRT ± pelvic nodes. Does not represent conventionally fractionated or moderately hypofractionated post-op RT, or intact-prostate treatment at the post-op cutoff.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: EXCALIBUR event count is not reported, so its AUCs rest on an unknown number of toxicity cases. Specificity was high at 0.50 in both cohorts, meaning the miss was in sensitivity, and the recalibration trades specificity back in a way the source does not quantify at 0.25.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The finding that generalizes is the **continuous score**, not a specific cutoff. Whether **0.25** is the right post-op trigger, and whether acting on it lowers GU toxicity, are both untested.

studies.interpretation:
The useful reading of this abstract separates two claims that the presentation bundles together. The first is that a germline mirSNP score built for intact-prostate SBRT still orders post-prostatectomy pts by their risk of late grade 2+ GU toxicity. That claim is reasonably supported: continuous AUCs of 0.814 in SCIMITAR and 0.824 in EXCALIBUR, with clearly separated median scores between pts with and without toxicity in both cohorts, and the model was applied unchanged rather than refit. The second claim is that 0.25 is the appropriate post-op decision threshold. That claim is much weaker, because the threshold was located by searching the same two cohorts for a cutoff meeting preset sensitivity and specificity targets and then reported with the AUCs it produced there. In-sample threshold selection almost always flatters dichotomized performance, and the candidate range the search returned (roughly 0.10 to 0.31) is wide enough that 0.25 should be read as one plausible point, not a calibrated constant.

The threshold shift itself is biologically and clinically plausible. A prostatectomy bed is a different organ-at-risk geometry from an intact gland: the bladder neck and vesicourethral anastomosis sit inside or abutting the target, and the urethra has already been surgically disrupted. A pt carrying a given germline susceptibility would be expected to cross into clinically apparent GU toxicity at a lower biological threshold in that setting. The fact that the intact 0.50 cutoff kept high specificity (0.985 and 0.926) while sensitivity collapsed is the pattern that explanation predicts: the score still ranks correctly, but too many susceptible post-op pts sit below a cutoff tuned for the intact gland.

For a radiation oncologist the more striking number may be the baseline rate. SCIMITAR reported 21/89 (23.6%) late grade 2+ GU events after 30 to 34 Gy in five fractions to the bed, and the conventional clinical candidates for predicting that, age, baseline pad use, IPSS and interval from surgery, carried no signal (all p > 0.2). That leaves the clinician with little to stratify on today, which is exactly the gap a validated germline score would fill. It also means the decision this could eventually move is substantive: whether a high-score pt is better served by a more conventional post-op fractionation, by tighter bladder-neck dosimetry, or simply by explicit counseling.

Several things would have to hold for the result to survive. The 0.25 cutoff needs testing in a third, independent post-op SBRT cohort with prespecified analysis. EXCALIBUR's event count, the toxicity grading scale and follow-up duration need to be reported, since late GU toxicity continues to accrue for years and AUCs on short follow-up can shift. The ± pelvic nodal fields in both cohorts introduce dose heterogeneity that was not modeled. And the score has not been tested in conventionally fractionated or moderately hypofractionated post-op RT, so nothing here speaks to whether high-risk pts would fare better with a different schedule. Until then, the defensible use is as a continuous risk input for counseling, not as a binary gate on who receives post-op SBRT.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: SCIMITAR logged 23.6% late G2+ GU AEs after 30-34 Gy in 5 fx to the bed, and no clinical factor tested predicted them (all p > 0.2). The germline score preserved ranking (continuous AUC 0.814/0.824), making it a candidate stratifier for bed SBRT counseling and planning once the 0.25 cutoff is externally validated.

open_questions: Does the 0.25 post-op threshold hold in an independent cohort?
Does the score predict GU toxicity with conventionally fractionated post-op RT?
Does risk-adaptive planning lower GU toxicity in high-score pts?

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Invited ASTRO 2026 review talk (Spratt), reported by UroToday. It brings together **POSEIDON** IPD meta-analysis, an adverse-feature IPD meta-analysis, **NRG GU006**, RTOG 0534 post-hoc PAM50 and MMAI analyses in RTOG 9601/0534.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Post-RP recurrent prostate cancer. GU006 enrolled **PSA 0.1-1.0 ng/mL, N0M0**. RTOG 0534 enrolled PSA 0.1-2.0 ng/mL, N0M0.

analysis_sections.body: GU006: salvage RT + **6 months apalutamide vs placebo**, blinded 1:1, stratified by margin status, pre-SRT PSA (<0.5 vs ≥0.5-1.0) and PAM50 subtype. POSEIDON compared RT ± HT and short-term (4-6mo) vs long-term (24mo) ADT.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: POSEIDON overall OS benefit from HT was **not statistically significant** (HR 0.87, p=0.06), and longer ADT gave **no extra benefit** (HR 0.96). Adverse feature count had **no significant interaction** with HT benefit.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: GU006 prospectively confirms the luminal B signal first suggested in retrospective subtyping work (Zhao, JAMA Oncol 2017) and seen again in RTOG 0534 post-hoc. Decipher carries Simon level 1B validation across RTOG 9601, RTOG 0534, NRG GU002 and NRG GU006.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-RP pts with rising PSA, N0M0, being considered for salvage RT ± short-course hormonal therapy. Does not represent N+/M+ disease, which SYMPHONY-FULL-SCORE will address.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: GU006 subgroup estimates are imprecise (luminal B MFS CI 0.07-0.95). The non-luminal B bPFS HR is reported with an **80% CI**. MMAI risk estimates are approximate curve reads with no prior independent validation step.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The talk's thesis is selection over intensification: PSA level and PAM50 subtype appear **predictive** of HT benefit, while adverse pathology is **prognostic only**. Optimal SRT fractionation, dose and nodal coverage stay open, and the SYMPHONY trials are designed to test them.

studies.interpretation:
The argument Spratt builds is that the post-prostatectomy hormone question has been answered for an average pt that does not exist. POSEIDON, pooling six randomized trials, gives the population-level answer: adding hormone therapy to post-operative RT did not reach statistical significance for OS, and stretching ADT from 4-6 to 24 months did nothing for OS. Read by itself, that sounds like de-escalation. The PSA-stratified rows say otherwise. The effect moves steadily from harm-leaning at PSA ≤0.20 (HR 1.14) to clear benefit above 0.50 ng/mL (HR 0.72 and 0.69). This is the pattern you would expect if pre-RT PSA tracks occult systemic burden, and it matters because the field has drifted toward early salvage at low PSA, exactly the stratum where HT showed nothing.

The adverse-feature meta-analysis is the useful negative control. Grade Group 4-5, SVI, ECE and positive margins are what most clinicians lean on when deciding on ADT. They predicted worse OS and MFS but did not modify HT benefit (interaction p=0.40 for OS). That separates prognosis from prediction more cleanly than most subgroup work does. A high-risk pathology report says the pt is likely to metastasize, not that ADT will prevent it.

GU006 is the strongest evidence in the talk because PAM50 was a stratification factor in a blinded, placebo-controlled design, not a retrospective slice. The luminal B MFS separation (95% vs 82% at 5 years) against flat non-luminal B curves is the cleanest predictive-biomarker signal in this setting. Two reasons for caution: the luminal B MFS interval is wide (0.07-0.95), so the size of the effect is uncertain even if its direction is not, and the non-luminal B bPFS estimate is reported with an 80% CI, which reads tighter than a 95% interval would. RTOG 0534's post-hoc PAM50 data agree in direction, but they are hypothesis-supporting, not confirmatory.

The MMAI digital pathology data are more preliminary than the talk's framing may suggest. The model went straight from training into randomized-trial validation without a standalone validation step, and the 12-year metastasis figures are approximate curve reads. Separation by HT benefit in MMAI-high RP pts is intriguing, but it is the weakest leg of the argument.

For the radiation oncologist, the practical shift concerns who gets the systemic add-on, not the RT itself. The RT parameters are still untested here: SYMPHONY's PRESTO, ADAGIO and CRESCENDO will test 5-fraction SBRT, dose reduction and elective nodal coverage. Until then, PSA level and PAM50 subtype are the defensible selectors for short-course intensification. Pathology count is not.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: For the salvage RT consult, pre-RT PSA ≤0.50 ng/mL showed no OS gain from adding HT (HR 1.14 and 0.94), and non-luminal B tumors gained nothing from apalutamide in GU006. Adverse pathology count was prognostic only. SYMPHONY will next test 5fx SBRT, dose reduction and elective nodal coverage.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Systematic review (183 articles) plus 3-round modified Delphi**, May 2025 to Feb 2026. Consensus = **≥75% agreement**; independent peer review, endorsed by ASTRO and ESTRO.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Panel of **48 experts from 15 countries**: 34 radiation oncologists, 7 medical oncologists, 7 urologic oncologists across North America, Europe, Asia and Australia. Scope: acute medical mgmt, RT technique, outlet obstruction, urology referral, HBOT.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **76%** favored moderate hypofx over SBRT at baseline **IPSS 15–19**; 85% endorsed a full bladder at sim and treatment. **No specific dose-volume constraint reached consensus.**

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Intact prostate: **alpha blockers first** for obstructive, **anti-spasmodics first** for irritative symptoms; post-RP: anti-spasmodics first. 80% against prophylactic medication; 80% add a 2nd agent rather than switch.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: MIRAGE was cited for margin reduction (**late G≥2 GU 51% → 27%** with 2-mm MRI-guided vs 4-mm CT-guided). CHHiP, PROFIT, RTOG 0415 and HYDRA were cited as showing no consistent late GU excess with moderate hypofx; RICH-ART supports HBOT for radiation cystitis.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men receiving definitive or post-prostatectomy RT for prostate cancer with acute or late GU adverse events. Does not represent GI toxicity, sexual function, or non-prostate pelvic RT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Several reported positions (74% IPSS ≥20 referral, 66% ≥12-wk wait, 52% SBRT after outlet procedure) fall **below the ≥75% consensus bar**. Panel is radonc-weighted, and this read comes from a conference summary, not the full manuscript.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Formalizes IPSS as a fractionation and referral gate and standardizes symptom-directed pharmacotherapy. It leaves **dose-volume constraints, urethral contouring reliability and RT-specific drug evidence** open; BEFORE, RadTARGET, RELIEF and DESTINATION-2 are named as ongoing.

studies.interpretation:
The most useful thing this guideline does is give radiation oncologists a shared vocabulary for something most departments already manage by habit. Acute GU toxicity after prostate RT has been treated with a drug ladder borrowed from benign urology, and the panel's main contribution on the pharmacologic side is to split that ladder by setting and symptom phenotype: obstructive versus irritative in the intact gland, and a separate post-prostatectomy pathway where alpha blockers are judged largely unhelpful. None of that rests on RT-specific randomized evidence, and the panel says so; the recommendations are a codification of reasonable practice rather than a demonstration that any agent changes symptom trajectory after radiation.

The technique recommendations carry more weight for planning. Using baseline IPSS to steer pts toward moderate hypofractionation rather than SBRT is consistent with how many programs already select SBRT candidates, but the vote distribution shows the threshold is softer than the headline suggests. A majority clustered at 15 to 19, yet a fifth chose 20 to 24, which means the cutoff is a convention rather than a validated inflection point. The cited moderate-hypofractionation literature (CHHiP, PROFIT, RTOG 0415, the HYDRA meta-analysis) supports the comparator arm being GU-safe; it does not establish that SBRT is worse in high-IPSS men, so the recommendation is a precautionary preference, not an evidence-derived contraindication.

MIRAGE is the one randomized technique result the guideline leans on, and its framing deserves care. That trial compared MRI-guided SBRT with 2-mm margins against CT-guided SBRT with 4-mm margins, so the GU benefit cannot be cleanly assigned to margin size versus the guidance platform. Citing it in a margin-reduction discussion is reasonable, but a reader without MR-linac access should not assume tighter CT-based margins reproduce the effect. The absence of any consensus dose-volume constraint is the more honest signal: after a systematic review of 183 articles, 48 experts could not agree on a bladder or urethral planning limit. Urethral sparing remains a planning decision without an agreed target.

Methodologically, a Delphi measures convergence of opinion, and the composition of the panel shapes where it converges. With radiation oncologists making up most of the panel, positions on outlet-procedure timing and referral thresholds reflect a predominantly radonc view of a urologic decision. Several reported items also fell short of the stated ≥75% threshold, including IPSS ≥20 referral, the 12-week post-procedure interval, and SBRT safety after an outlet procedure; these should be read as majority leanings, not consensus, and the conference summary does not always make that distinction clear.

What would make this guideline wrong is fairly specific. If the ongoing trials named (BEFORE, RadTARGET, RELIEF, DESTINATION-2) show that prophylactic pharmacotherapy or urethra-directed planning materially reduces GU toxicity, the anti-prophylaxis position and the agnosticism on constraints would both need revision. The working group frames the document as living, which is the correct posture for a framework built mostly on extrapolation. For now it standardizes communication and referral more than it changes outcomes.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Baseline IPSS now formally gates fractionation: 76% favored moderate hypofx over SBRT at IPSS 15–19, with full bladder endorsed by 85%. MIRAGE margins were cited, but no bladder or urethral dose-volume constraint reached consensus, so planning limits stay institutional.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: For urologic surgeons, the timing question is answered: 94% would wait ≥8 weeks after an outlet procedure before RT, and 85% would consider a prophylactic procedure for severe LUTS, but 95% not when irritative symptoms predominate. The IPSS ≥20 referral trigger drew 74%, just below the consensus bar.
